Encode runs of repeated characters as a count and the character, and decode them back.

<a class="nomi-rough-badge" href="#rough-edges">rough edges</a> Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/run-length-encoding) (MIT). Listed under [Encoding & Ciphers](/examples/?subject=encoding-and-ciphers).

```nomi-run
// FILE: run_length_encoding.nomi
import std/regex.Regex

/// `text` with each run of a repeated character written as its length and
/// the character once. A character that is not repeated keeps no count.
pub fn encode(text: String) -> String {
    text
    |> Iter.chunk_by(fn letter -> letter)
    |> Iter.map(encode_run)
    |> String.join()
}

fn encode_run(run: List<String>) -> String {
    case run {
        [letter] -> letter
        [letter, .._] -> "${Iter.count(run)}${letter}"
        [] -> unreachable "chunk_by never yields an empty run"
    }
}

/// The text `encode` was given for `encoded`: each character is repeated as
/// many times as the number before it says, or once when there is none.
pub fn decode(encoded: String) -> String {
    encoded
    |> String.captures_all(Regex`(\d*)(\D)`)
    |> Iter.map(decode_run)
    |> String.join()
}

fn decode_run(groups: List<Maybe<String>>) -> String {
    case groups {
        [Some(count), Some(letter)] -> {
            times = String.to_int(count) |> Maybe.with_default(1)
            String.repeat(letter, times)
        }

        _ ->
            unreachable `(\d*)(\D) always has two groups, and both take part`
    }
}

// FILE: run_length_encoding_test.nomi
import run_length_encoding

test "run-length encode a string" {
    cases = [
        #("empty string", "", ""),
        #("single characters only are encoded without count", "XYZ", "XYZ"),
        #("string with no single characters", "AABBBCCCC", "2A3B4C"),
        #(
            "single characters mixed with repeated characters",
            "WWWWWWWWWWWWBWWWWWWWWWWWWBBBWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWB",
            "12WB12W3B24WB",
        ),
        #("multiple whitespace mixed in string", "  hsqq qww  ", "2 hs2q q2w2 "),
        #("lowercase characters", "aabbbcccc", "2a3b4c"),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, text, expected), description {
        assert run_length_encoding.encode(text) == expected
    }
}

test "run-length decode a string" {
    cases = [
        #("empty string", "", ""),
        #("single characters only", "XYZ", "XYZ"),
        #("string with no single characters", "2A3B4C", "AABBBCCCC"),
        #(
            "single characters with repeated characters",
            "12WB12W3B24WB",
            "WWWWWWWWWWWWBWWWWWWWWWWWWBBBWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWB",
        ),
        #("multiple whitespace mixed in string", "2 hs2q q2w2 ", "  hsqq qww  "),
        #("lowercase string", "2a3b4c", "aabbbcccc"),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, encoded, expected), description {
        assert run_length_encoding.decode(encoded) == expected
    }
}

test "encode and then decode" {
    text = "zzz ZZ  zZ"

    assert text |> run_length_encoding.encode() |> run_length_encoding.decode() == text
}
```

## How it's written

- `encode` is `Iter.chunk_by` on the string's graphemes, then each run written out by `encode_run`, then `String.join`.
- `decode` reads the runs with ``String.captures_all(Regex`(\d*)(\D)`)``: an optional count, then one character. `decode_run` repeats the character `count` times, or once when the count group matched empty. The other way is an `Iter.reduce` over graphemes that threads `#(count, text)` and builds the count digit by digit; the pattern is clearer because it states the encoded format in one line, where the reducer spreads it over a tuple accumulator and an `if count == 0` fallback. The cost is that `\D` matches one code point, not one grapheme, so a run of a character written with a combining mark would decode wrongly; the canonical cases are all single code points.
- Each canonical group is a test named by the group's description, holding one `subtests` table; the round-trip case is a plain test.
- The arms the types require but the code never reaches are `unreachable` with the invariant as the reason (style §28): `[] -> unreachable "chunk_by never yields an empty run"` in `encode_run`, and the `_` arm of `decode_run`, which the pattern's two always-participating groups rule out. A made-up `""` there would hide a bug in either.

## Rough edges

Where Nomi made this exercise harder than it should be. Each is an open question for the language, not a settled answer.

- **Longer than it should be.** `Iter.chunk_by` returns each run as a `List<T>`, which is never empty, but `case run` must still handle `[]` to be exhaustive. Its arm is an `unreachable`, which says what is true, but it is still an arm to write. Rust's `chunk_by` yields slices with the same problem; Gleam's `list.chunk` too. Elixir's `Enum.chunk_by` is untyped. A non-empty list type, or `chunk_by` yielding `#(first, rest)`, would remove the arm.
- **Longer than it should be.** `String.captures_all` returns each match's groups as a `List<Maybe<String>>`, so `decode_run` must handle shapes the pattern `(\d*)(\D)` cannot produce, with an `unreachable` arm: the type says neither that there are two groups nor that both always take part. Rust's `captures_iter` and Go's `FindAllStringSubmatch` have the same gap; a typed capture (a tuple per pattern) would remove the arm.
